title: Part 2: Anita Rutter
content_html:
The Arrival of Anita Rutter

Anita Rutter enters the novel like a force of nature. She is blonde, bold, foul-mouthed, and utterly fearless — everything that Meena is not. For Meena, who has spent her childhood trying to fit in, Anita represents a thrilling new possibility: the chance to belong to the most exciting person in Tollington. Their friendship is immediate and intense, built on Meena’s admiration and Anita’s need for a loyal follower.

Syal presents Anita as both magnetic and dangerous from the outset. She is the kind of girl who commands attention — older children defer to her, younger ones fear her. Meena is drawn to Anita’s rebelliousness because it offers an escape from the careful, polite world of the Kumar household. Where Meena’s parents value education, restraint, and cultural pride, Anita values toughness, streetwise savvy, and social dominance.

Key Fact

The friendship between Meena and Anita is built on an unequal power dynamic. Anita leads and Meena follows. Meena is drawn to Anita’s confidence, but from the start Anita uses Meena’s eagerness to please as a tool for control.

Why Meena Is Drawn to Anita

Meena’s attraction to Anita is rooted in her desire to escape the constraints of her dual identity. At home, she is expected to be a good Indian girl — respectful, studious, obedient. With Anita, she can be wild, rude, and free. The friendship offers Meena a version of the English childhood she envies: playing in the streets, talking back to adults, being part of the gang. As Meena puts it, “I wanted to be them. I wanted their life.”

But Syal is careful to show that Meena’s admiration is based on misunderstanding. What Meena sees as freedom is actually neglect. Anita’s boldness comes not from confidence but from the absence of boundaries. She has learned to fend for herself because no one at home is looking after her.

Anita’s home life is the dark mirror of Meena’s. While the Kumar household is warm, structured, and loving, the Rutter household is chaotic and emotionally barren. Anita’s mother, Deirdre Rutter, is a figure of neglect — more concerned with her own social life and string of unsuitable partners than with her daughters. Anita’s father is absent. Anita and her younger sister Tracey are left to raise themselves.

Syal uses the Rutter household to explore the class dynamics of Tollington. The Rutters represent the struggling white working class — the poverty, the broken family structures, the lack of aspiration that traps people in cycles of deprivation. Anita’s behaviour is not simply “bad” — it is a survival strategy developed by a child who has been failed by every adult in her life.

The Power Dynamic

The friendship between Meena and Anita is never one of equals. Anita is always in charge: she decides what they do, where they go, and who else is included. Meena accepts this subordinate role because being Anita’s follower is better than being alone. She tolerates Anita’s cruelty, her casual put-downs, and her habit of dropping Meena whenever someone more useful comes along.

This dynamic mirrors the wider racial power structure of 1960s Britain. Just as Meena must suppress her identity to be accepted by Anita, immigrant communities were expected to assimilate — to become invisible, to not make a fuss. Syal uses the microcosm of a childhood friendship to expose the macro-level dynamics of race and belonging in post-war England.

Key Fact

Syal uses the unequal friendship to mirror the racial dynamics of 1960s Britain. Meena must suppress her cultural identity to be accepted by Anita, just as immigrant families were expected to assimilate into white British society without complaint.

Sam Lowbridge

Sam Lowbridge is one of the novel’s most important secondary characters. He is an older teenager who hangs around the village with a gang of boys, exuding a threatening masculinity. Meena initially has a childish crush on Sam, finding him exciting and dangerous. But Sam is also the character most explicitly associated with racism — his views echo Enoch Powell’s rhetoric, and he becomes increasingly aggressive towards Meena’s family as the novel progresses.

Sam and Anita are linked throughout the novel. They share a working-class background, a lack of parental guidance, and a tendency towards aggressive self-assertion. While Meena is initially blind to the danger Sam represents, Syal gradually reveals that the racism Meena encounters is not just words — it is backed by the threat of violence. Sam’s character embodies the way that economic deprivation, poor education, and political manipulation (through figures like Powell) can turn ordinary people into agents of hatred.

Crucially, Anita’s association with Sam forces Meena to confront an uncomfortable truth: the world she so desperately wants to belong to may not want her. The friendship that promised belonging ultimately forces Meena to recognise that some people will never accept her because of her race.

Syal uses Anita and Sam to present the intertwined nature of class, race, and power in Tollington. Both characters are products of a broken system, but their responses to deprivation take different forms: Anita manipulates individuals, while Sam targets entire communities.

title: Exam Technique
content_html:
The Modern Text Essay: What Examiners Reward

Modern text essay questions on DNA ask you to write about how Kelly presents a theme, character, or idea across the whole play. You will usually be offered a choice of two questions and must answer one in full.

Crucially, modern text papers are typically closed book and do not provide an extract. You must write about the whole play from memory. This makes the modern text essay one of the most demanding parts of your literature course, because everything depends on what you can remember. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark weightings and time allowance that apply to you.

Key Fact

A strong modern text essay on DNA delivers three things: a sustained, personal response to the play supported by references from memory; context (Milgram, 2008 youth violence, moral philosophy, Connections programme) embedded in your analysis; and clear, fluent academic writing. Close language analysis is usually not the focus of this question.

What Each Strand of Your Essay Needs to Do

Argument and response: Have a clear thesis and support it with textual evidence. Maintain an analytical style throughout — every paragraph should develop your reading of the play.

Context: Show understanding of the relationships between the text and the contexts in which it was written. For DNA, this means: Kelly’s response to 2008 youth violence, Milgram’s obedience experiment, gang culture, moral philosophy, and the National Theatre Connections programme. Context must be embedded in your analysis, not bolted on as a separate paragraph.

Writing quality: Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose, and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation. This rewards clear, fluent academic writing.

Identifying language devices (“Kelly uses a metaphor…”) is usually not what earns marks on a modern text essay. You can, and should, discuss structural and dramatic choices — staging, silence, the four-act structure, the field as a recurring space — where they support your argument about Kelly’s ideas. But the focus is on what Kelly is saying (ideas, themes, context) rather than a technique checklist. Treat every structural observation as an opportunity to say more about meaning.

Quotation Strategies for a Closed-Book Exam

Since you do not have the text in front of you, you need practical strategies for incorporating evidence. You do not need to memorise long quotations. Examiners reward relevant references to the play, which can take several forms:

  • Short quotations (1–4 words): These are the most effective for a closed-book exam. Examples: Phil’s “silence,” Leah’s “bonobos,” John Tate banning the word “dead,” Cathy going into “television.”
  • Paraphrased references: Describe a specific moment accurately. Example: “When Phil calmly outlines his plan while eating an ice cream, Kelly contrasts his detachment with the group’s panic.”
  • Structural references: Refer to the play’s form and design. Example: “The replacement of Leah with Richard in the final field scene shows that the play’s moral conscience has been silenced.”
Key Fact

For a closed-book exam, memorise short quotations (1–4 words) and specific moments. You do not need long quotations. Examiners reward accurate paraphrased references to the play just as much as direct quotation. Aim for 2–3 key references per paragraph.

Essay Planning: The 5-Minute Plan

Assume you have around 45 minutes for the modern text question. Spend the first 5 minutes planning. A strong plan should include:

  • Thesis: One sentence stating your overall argument. Example: “Kelly presents guilt as widespread but ultimately meaningless, because no character translates their guilt into action.”
  • 3–4 paragraph topics: Each covering a different character, moment, or aspect of the play. Aim for chronological coverage (early play, middle, end) to show whole-text knowledge.
  • Key references: 2–3 short quotations or specific moments for each paragraph.
  • Context links: One context point per paragraph (e.g., Milgram, 2008 youth culture, Connections programme).

Model paragraph (for the question: “How does Kelly present ideas about guilt in DNA?”):

“Kelly presents guilt as something that is felt but never acted upon, suggesting that moral awareness without courage is ultimately meaningless. Leah is the character most consumed by guilt, delivering long monologues in the field about bonobos — apes who resolve conflict through empathy rather than violence — as an alternative to the group’s behaviour. However, Phil’s refusal to respond renders her moral questioning powerless. Leah knows the cover-up is wrong, yet she never defies Phil or leaves the group. Kelly may be drawing on Milgram’s 1963 obedience experiment, which showed that most people will follow immoral instructions when an authority figure takes charge: Leah, like Milgram’s distressed participants, continues to comply despite her visible anguish. Her disappearance in Act 4 confirms that in Kelly’s world, the voice of conscience is silenced, not because it is wrong, but because it lacks the power to be heard.”

What this paragraph does well: It opens with a clear point about the theme. It uses a short keyword reference (“bonobos”) and a paraphrased moment (Phil’s silence, Leah’s disappearance) rather than long quotations. Context (Milgram) is embedded naturally, not bolted on. It ends with analysis of Kelly’s wider message.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The most common mistakes in the modern text essay are:

  • Retelling the story: The examiner knows the plot. Every sentence should analyse, not describe. Use “Kelly presents…” or “Kelly suggests…” rather than “Then Phil says…”
  • Bolting on context: Do not write a separate paragraph about Milgram or 2008. Weave context into your analysis: “Kelly, writing in 2008 during a period of intense public anxiety about youth violence, uses Phil’s calm detachment to show how…”
  • Technique-spotting: You can mention dramatic choices (structure, staging, dialogue style) to support your argument, but do not write paragraphs about “Kelly uses a metaphor to…”
  • Only writing about one part of the play: You must show knowledge of the whole text. Reference events or characters from at least three different parts of the play.

title: Part 3: Growing Apart
content_html:
Racism Comes Into the Open

In the first half of the novel, the racism Meena encounters is mostly subtle — whispered comments, awkward silences, the feeling of being watched. But as the story progresses, Syal strips away this veneer of politeness. The racism becomes explicit, public, and threatening. The turning point is Sam Lowbridge’s speech at the village fete, where he declares “We are the British” and openly attacks the presence of immigrants in Tollington.

This moment is devastating for Meena because it shatters her illusion of belonging. She has spent the novel trying to fit in, trying to be accepted as one of Tollington’s children. Sam’s speech makes it brutally clear that, in the eyes of people like him, she will never belong. The phrase “We are the British” deliberately excludes Meena and her family — it draws a line between “us” and “them” based entirely on race.

Key Fact

Sam Lowbridge’s declaration “We are the British” at the village fete is the novel’s most explicit moment of racism. It echoes Enoch Powell’s inflammatory rhetoric and forces Meena to confront the reality that her race makes her an outsider in the community she calls home.

The Mines Closing

Tollington’s economic decline is a crucial backdrop to the rising racial tension. The coal mines and factories that sustained the Black Country for generations are closing, and the community feels abandoned. Jobs are disappearing, prospects are shrinking, and there is a pervasive sense of resentment that needs a target.

Syal is careful to show that racism does not exist in a vacuum. Characters like Sam Lowbridge are products of economic deprivation — their anger at losing their livelihoods gets redirected towards immigrant families who are seen as competition for scarce resources. This does not excuse racism, but it explains the social conditions that allow it to flourish. The novel asks the reader to understand how structural inequality breeds prejudice.

Scapegoating is a key concept in the novel. When communities face hardship, they often look for someone to blame. In Tollington, immigrant families become the scapegoat for problems caused by deindustrialisation and government neglect. Sam’s anger is real — his community is genuinely suffering — but it is misdirected at the Kumars rather than at the economic forces that are actually destroying Tollington.

This pattern — economic hardship breeding racial resentment — was widespread across industrial England in the 1960s and 1970s. Syal uses Tollington as a case study to show how ordinary people can be radicalised by poverty and political rhetoric. The closing of the mines is not just a plot detail; it is the engine driving the novel’s racial conflict.

Meena’s Illness

A major turning point in the novel is Meena’s leg injury, which confines her to bed for an extended period. This enforced stillness is transformative. For the first time, Meena is removed from the social pressures of Tollington — from Anita, from the need to perform, from the constant effort of fitting in. The illness creates a liminal space in which Meena can think, reflect, and begin to see her life more clearly.

During her recovery, Meena starts to question the friendship with Anita and to recognise the racism she has been ignoring or minimising. The illness functions as a metaphor for the painful process of growing up — the shedding of childhood innocence and the development of a more mature, honest understanding of the world.

Key Fact

Meena’s illness is both a literal event and a metaphor. It removes her from Anita’s influence, forces reflection, and marks the beginning of her emotional and psychological maturation. After the illness, Meena begins to see Tollington — and herself — more honestly.

Nanima’s Visit

The arrival of Nanima (Meena’s maternal grandmother) during Meena’s illness is one of the novel’s most emotionally significant moments. Nanima does not speak English, but she communicates through touch, food, stories, and the sheer force of her presence. She represents everything Meena has been running from — her Indian heritage, her family history, the Punjabi language, the deep roots of a culture that stretches back generations.

Nanima’s visit coincides with Meena’s period of reflection, and the combination is powerful. For the first time, Meena begins to see her heritage not as an embarrassment but as a source of strength and identity. Nanima’s stories about Partition — the traumatic division of India and Pakistan in 1947 — give Meena a sense of her family’s history and resilience that she has never had before.

The middle section of the novel sees Meena in full identity crisis. She has tried to be English and been rejected. She has neglected her Indian heritage and now feels disconnected from it. She is caught between Sam’s “We are the British” (which excludes her) and her family’s quiet insistence that “This is also my home” (which claims belonging on different terms). Meena confesses: “I did not have a name for what I felt.”

This line captures the essence of the novel’s exploration of cultural duality. Meena’s confusion is not simply about choosing between two cultures — it is about finding a way to be both. Nanima’s visit begins to show her that this is possible: that she can be Indian and English, that belonging does not require the erasure of one identity for the sake of another.

title: Structure, Setting & Narrative Technique
content_html:
Structure and Narrative Technique

For the Edexcel exam, understanding how Gavin tells the story is just as important as understanding what happens. Questions may ask you to explore how Gavin uses structure, setting or narrative techniques to present ideas. This lesson equips you with the analytical vocabulary and structural awareness to write confidently about form and craft.

The Dual Timeline

Coram Boy is structured around a dual timeline. Part 1 is set in the early 1740s and follows Meshak and Otis alongside the Ashbrook family. Part 2 jumps forward to the late 1740s and follows Aaron at the Foundling Hospital. Part 3 brings these timelines together when Aaron’s true identity is revealed. This structure creates sustained dramatic irony — the reader knows the connection between the two timelines long before the characters do.

Key Fact

The dual timeline is not just a way of organising events — it is a structural argument. By separating the privileged Ashbrook world from the foundling world, Gavin forces the reader to see how class divides keep people apart even when they are intimately connected.

Multiple Perspectives

Gavin uses a third-person omniscient narrator who moves between different characters’ perspectives. We see events through Meshak’s bewildered, emotional viewpoint; through Otis’s cold, calculating mind; through Alexander’s conflicted ambition; and through Aaron’s search for identity. This shifting perspective allows Gavin to build empathy for multiple characters simultaneously and to create tension by revealing information to the reader that individual characters do not have.

The most powerful use of perspective is through Meshak. When we see the buried babies through his eyes, the horror is intensified because Meshak does not intellectualise or rationalise what he sees — he simply feels it. His emotional directness cuts through any distance the reader might otherwise maintain.

Gavin draws on the Gothic tradition throughout Coram Boy. The landscapes Meshak and Otis travel through are dark, isolated and threatening. The buried babies create an atmosphere of horror that borders on the supernatural — Meshak hears them crying, and the reader is never entirely sure whether this is psychological trauma or something more. The Gothic elements serve a thematic purpose: they prevent the reader from distancing themselves from the cruelty. Gavin uses Gothic imagery to insist that the reader feels the horror of child trafficking rather than merely understanding it intellectually.

Setting as Theme

Every major setting in the novel carries thematic significance. Ashbrook House represents privilege, tradition and the constraints of class. The open roads where Otis and Meshak travel represent lawlessness, danger and the margins of society. The Foundling Hospital represents institutional care — safety without love, rescue without identity. London represents opportunity and culture (through Handel and music) but also the anonymous cruelty of a large city where children can disappear.

Key Fact

Gavin uses settings symbolically: each location represents a different relationship between society and children. Ashbrook House protects its own children through privilege; the Foundling Hospital protects abandoned children through charity; the open road offers no protection at all. The novel asks which model of care is adequate — and the answer is none of them.

Music as Structural Motif

Music is not just a theme in Coram Boy — it functions as a structural motif that binds the novel together. Alexander’s passion for music in Part 1 connects to Aaron’s singing voice in Part 2, with Handel as the bridging figure. Gavin uses the Messiah performances at the Foundling Hospital to bring characters physically together. Music also provides the novel’s emotional register — moments of beauty and transcendence that contrast with the darkness of the child-trafficking plot.

Gavin weaves real historical facts into the fiction so seamlessly that the line between history and invention becomes blurred. Thomas Coram, Handel, the Foundling Hospital and the practice of baby farming are all real — Meshak, Otis, Alexander and Aaron are fictional. By grounding her fictional characters in real historical settings and institutions, Gavin gives the novel the weight of historical truth. This technique makes the reader feel that these events could have happened, which intensifies the emotional impact. For AO3, you can discuss how Gavin uses historical research to create verisimilitude — making the fictional world feel authentic.

Dramatic Irony as a Structural Tool

The most sustained structural technique in Coram Boy is dramatic irony. From Part 1, the reader knows that Meshak saved Alexander and Melissa’s baby. Throughout Part 2, the reader watches Aaron grow up at the Foundling Hospital, knowing his true parentage while he does not. This creates a constant undercurrent of tension: the reader is waiting for the characters to discover what we already know. Gavin sustains this irony across hundreds of pages, which is a remarkable structural achievement — the resolution in Part 3, when the truth finally emerges, is powerful precisely because the reader has been anticipating it for so long.

Being able to discuss structure, setting and narrative technique gives your essay analytical depth. Examiners reward students who can explain how Gavin achieves her effects, not just describe what happens in the story.
